section_summary: This section assembles diplomatic reporting, internal memoranda, telegrams, cross-reference sheets, and propaganda enclosures from 1934–1939 concerning Japanese publicity, intelligence gathering, espionage fears, and anti-foreign mobilization. Subjects include patriotic clothing, overseas naval propaganda, questioning about Singapore’s defenses, an attempted sale of intelligence in Taiwan, anti-spy exhibitions and press campaigns, and propaganda connected with the Sino-Japanese War. The largest subfile is a translated Japanese anti-Semitic pamphlet that advances extensive conspiracy theories and racist allegations about Jews, governments, finance, war, and medicine.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on Japanese cultural publicity abroad
subfiles.about: Discusses plans for Japanese cultural attachés and study institutes in major Western cities.
subfiles.summary: The fragment argues that greater Western knowledge of Japan could improve understanding of Far Eastern problems. It nevertheless warns that proposed attachés, libraries, and institutes might become instruments of Japanese propaganda and thereby undermine their stated cultural purpose.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Kobe despatch No. 396
subfiles.to: Under Secretary of State; Mr. Dunn
subfiles.about: Evaluates a Kobe report concerning patriotic motifs on Japanese women's clothing.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum characterizes the clothing as an example of businesses exploiting popular patriotism. It compares the phenomenon with theatrical promotions after the Mukden Incident and concludes that too much significance may have been attached to it.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 396: Anti-Foreign Activities at Kobe, Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the manufacture and sale of patriotic kimonos bearing military and anti-foreign designs.
subfiles.summary: Donovan describes women's and children's kimonos decorated with battleships, aircraft, antiaircraft crews, flags, and slogans anticipating a 1936 crisis. Consular clerk Carey J. Scott traced the designs to Osaka firms and learned that they derived from an exhibition honoring General Araki. Some designs asserted Japanese superiority over Britain and the United States; two purchased kimonos were forwarded to Ambassador Grew for possible transmission to the Department.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese naval propaganda telegram
subfiles.about: Cross-references Grew's telegram on the overseas distribution of Japanese naval propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The note directs readers to telegram No. 268 in another decimal-file location. It records the Navy's dispatch of 10,000 propaganda pamphlets to Japanese societies and schools across the Pacific and plans for a further printing.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 268 on Japanese naval propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Navy Department's mass distribution of propaganda pamphlets abroad.
subfiles.summary: Grew states that the Navy's publicity section sent 10,000 copies of several naval propaganda pamphlets on December 3. Recipients included Japanese societies and schools in the South Seas, Hawaii, the Pacific Coast of the United States, Canada, and elsewhere, with another 10,000-copy pamphlet planned.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese propaganda publications distributed at Rome
subfiles.doc_type: military attaché report with cover notation
subfiles.about: Describes propaganda publications supplied by the Japanese military attaché at Rome.
subfiles.summary: The report says the Japanese military attaché sent the office several English-language publications, including Present-Day Japan, a report on Manchuria, and Japan at a Glance. It regards the publications as government-inspired and notes their presentation of Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations and other material intended to cultivate favorable opinion.

subfiles.title: Voluntary Report No. 23: Japanese Intelligence Methods
subfiles.from: Jack Cocke, American Vice Consul, Nantes
subfiles.about: Relates an Argentine consul's encounter with Japanese police questioning about Singapore's defenses.
subfiles.summary: Leoni states that Japanese officials inspected his baggage and later questioned him about British fortifications and airport construction at Singapore. He answered evasively and offered broader opinions about Japan's strategic position. The report concludes with his view that Soviet military preparations in Siberia and at Vladivostok made Russia an effective buffer protecting Western powers from Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on the Japanese Secret Service
subfiles.about: Cross-references a special report and newspaper clipping on the Japanese secret service.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to Special Report No. D-1584 filed elsewhere. That report enclosed an article from the August 23, 1935 issue of Cyrano concerning the Japanese secret service and its fields of action.

subfiles.title: File note on women, foreigners, and alleged espionage
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on alleged links between Japanese women's contacts with foreigners and espionage.
subfiles.summary: The note says selection of Japan for the 1940 Olympic Games intensified campaigns against espionage. It also records a campaign to protect Japanese womanhood from supposedly immoral foreigners.

subfiles.title: File note on propaganda among foreigners in the Far East
subfiles.about: Cross-references correspondence illustrating an unusual form of Japanese propaganda among foreign residents.
subfiles.summary: The note describes a December 15 letter sent to J. B. Emmert by a fellow stamp collector in Japan. The referenced correspondence was cited as evidence of the lengths and distinctive methods used in disseminating propaganda to foreigners in the Far East.

subfiles.title: File note on Why? Who? How?
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Japanese question-and-answer pamphlet on the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the transmission of Why? Who? How? Questions and Answers on the Conflict. The pamphlet was issued by the Foreign Affairs Association of Japan as propaganda concerning the Sino-Japanese conflict.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese occupation propaganda at Chefoo
subfiles.about: Cross-references correspondence about pamphlets dropped after Japanese forces took Chefoo.
subfiles.summary: The note records that Japanese forces occupied Chefoo on February 3. Aircraft subsequently dropped pamphlets containing advice about the evacuation of foreigners.

subfiles.title: File note on a Japanese military propaganda leaflet
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Mukden despatch transmitting a Japanese propaganda leaflet on the current crisis.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes the leaflet as a document contributing to an understanding of the Japanese military mind. It refers readers to Consulate despatch No. 205, which enclosed a copy.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on an attempted sale of information at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Comments on Consul Warner's handling of an unidentified Japanese man's offer to sell information.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Warner's notification of the Taihoku provincial authorities and his suggestion that the consular employee set a trap if the visitor returned. It concludes that Warner may have been overly eager to cooperate with the Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding memorandum on an offer to sell information
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports an unidentified Japanese visitor's effort to sell information to consular clerk Tan Ko-Heng.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports the approach and supplies provincial official Wataru Shibaoka with information about a possibly related Ri Kin-sho of Manila. He advises Tan to learn what the visitor has to sell, negotiate for delivery, and arrange for police to seize him afterward. Warner promises to report further developments.

subfiles.title: Memorandum by Tan Ko-Heng on the unidentified Japanese visitor
subfiles.about: Provides Tan's firsthand account of the visitor who offered to sell information.
subfiles.summary: Tan says the visitor claimed to have come from Kobe and to have been referred by Ri Kin-sho, a Taiwan-born Manila grocer. The man refused to give his own name, asked whether Tan wished to buy information, and spoke in a manner Tan associated with secret or military police. Fearing a provocation and immediate arrest, Tan displayed no interest.

subfiles.title: Internal note on Peiping's annual developments report
subfiles.about: Recommends reading Peiping's report on political, military, economic, and financial developments during 1937.
subfiles.summary: The brief routing note draws attention to the Embassy's February 7 despatch. It recommends that the addressees read the full report because of its treatment of significant developments during 1937.

subfiles.title: Letter commending Laurence E. Salisbury's despatch
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping
subfiles.about: Praises Salisbury's report on developments during 1937.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to Peiping despatch No. 1541 of February 7, prepared by First Secretary Laurence E. Salisbury. It asks Johnson to inform Salisbury that the despatch's clear, logical, and comprehensive presentation made it exceptionally valuable.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Osaka's anti-spy campaign report
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the final paragraph of Osaka's March 30 report on anti-spy measures.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that most of the information in Osaka's report had already been reported elsewhere. It nevertheless suggests that the reader examine the report's final paragraph.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Japanese Anti-Spy Measures
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, American Consul General
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential report on Japanese anti-spy measures.
subfiles.summary: Makinson encloses a report entitled Japanese Anti-Spy Measures for the Embassy's information. Copies were also distributed to the Department of State and the supervising consulate general at Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Japanese Anti-Spy Measures
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Surveys an Osaka anti-spy exhibition, press propaganda, and restrictions affecting foreigners.
subfiles.summary: The report describes a government-sponsored exhibition that linked patriotism and militarism with warnings against communism, labor agitation, foreign propaganda, and espionage. Displays portrayed social contact with foreigners, railway conversations, and public investigations as possible security threats, prompting concern from the British consul about obstruction of legitimate trade inquiries. Makinson also reviews an Osaka Mainichi article alleging British, French, Soviet, and American espionage and notes restrictions discouraging foreigners from cruising, photographing, driving, or traveling freely.

subfiles.title: File note on Tokyo's wartime thought-control exhibit
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report and press clipping on a Tokyo wartime thought-control exhibition.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to despatch No. 2799 on the February 1938 exhibition. The referenced despatch enclosed a February 27 Japan Advertiser clipping titled Big Crowds Attend Propaganda Exhibit.

subfiles.title: File note on The Cases for Japan and China
subfiles.about: Cross-references a booklet presenting competing cases for Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The file note records enclosure of The Cases For Japan And China, distributed by the Foreign Affairs Association of Japan. It characterizes the booklet as a sample of improved Japanese propaganda.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese handbills over Foochow
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on Japanese propaganda handbills dropped over Foochow.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the scattering of Japanese propaganda handbills over the city. It specifies that Japanese aircraft distributed the leaflets.

subfiles.title: File note on America's Share in Japan's War Guilt
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch transmitting a pamphlet opposing American assistance to Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to Shanghai despatch No. 1829 concerning propaganda against American aid to Japan's war effort. The despatch transmitted a pamphlet titled America's Share in Japan's War Guilt.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 466
subfiles.about: Evaluates a translated anti-Semitic pamphlet enclosed by the Yokohama consulate.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the nineteen-page translation makes allegations about supposed Jewish ancestry among American presidents. It dismisses the work as unintelligent and recommends no action, noting its dietary prescription as the proposed escape from alleged Jewish influence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 466: Anti-Jewish Propaganda in Japan
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese text and translation of an anti-Semitic pamphlet sold in Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports that the pamphlet had recently appeared on Yokohama newsstands amid other publications imitating anti-Semitic propaganda abroad. He highlights its claims about the supposed Jewish ancestry of American presidents. Although Japanese censorship could suppress such material, he doubts it would do so while official publicity emphasized cultural ties with Germany.

subfiles.title: The China Incident and the Activity of the Jews
subfiles.from: Joichi Sakurazawa, International Political and Economic Association
subfiles.about: Presents an anti-Semitic interpretation of the Sino-Japanese War, world politics, finance, culture, and health.
subfiles.summary: Sakurazawa claims that Jews secretly control governments, banks, newspapers, industry, entertainment, science, and political movements across Europe, the United States, the Soviet Union, China, and Japan. He uses numerous false, contradictory, or distorted assertions about named public figures and events to portray the China conflict as part of an inevitable struggle between Japan and an alleged global Jewish conspiracy. The closing sections connect these conspiracy theories to Sakurazawa's advocacy of Japanese food and nutrition, presenting diet and national health as Japan's principal defense. The document is an extended example of Japanese anti-Semitic propaganda rather than a factual account of the people and institutions it describes.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3742: Report of Conditions in Japan during February 1939
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan for February 1939.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards monthly Report No. 149 pursuant to a 1926 Department instruction. Copies were distributed to diplomatic and consular posts across East Asia and to the commander-in-chief of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet, but the substantive enclosure is not present in this section.

subfiles.title: File note on proposed industrial-espionage legislation
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on proposed Japanese legislation to suppress industrial espionage.
subfiles.summary: The note points to despatch No. 3714 in another file location. The referenced report discussed a proposed bill and the fifteen categories of protected information listed in its second article as reported by the press.
